Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:6: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said in the name of Rabbi Shmuel: see the humility that is in the Holy One, blessed be He - what is written? (Ezekiel 44:2), "and the LORD said to me, this gate shall be shut, it shall not be opened," and so on. A king of flesh and blood, his honor is to enter through a great gate, not through a small gate - but the Holy One, blessed be He, enters in His glory through a small gate - hence, "and Your humility has made me great."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:7: Ben Azzai said, a king of flesh and blood, when he mentions his own name, [does so] briefly - but the Holy One, blessed be He, mentions His deeds and afterward mentions His Name, as it is said (Genesis 1:1), "in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:8: Another explanation: "and You have given me the shield of Your salvation" (Psalms 18:36) - "fear not, Abram, I am a shield to you" (Genesis 15:1). "And Your right hand has upheld me" - in the fiery furnace, among the kings, and in famine, as it is written, "the utterance of the LORD to my Lord, sit at My right hand" (Psalms 110:1). "And Your humility has made me great" - how great was the humility, that He would sit while the Shechinah stood, as it is written (Genesis 18:1), "and the LORD appeared to him at the terebinths of Mamre, while he sat at the entrance of the tent" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:9: Further, they said in Megillah (31a) - these are their own words: Rabbi Yochanan said, wherever you find the might of the Holy One, blessed be He, there you find His humility beside it - this is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and stated a third time in the Writings. In the Torah (Deuteronomy 10:17), "for the LORD your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords," and it is written after it, "who executes judgment for the orphan and the widow." Repeated in the Prophets, as it is said (Isaiah 57:15), "for thus says the High and Exalted One," and it is written after it, "and with the contrite and humble of spirit." Stated a third time in the Writings, as it is written (Psalms 68:5), "extol Him who rides upon the clouds, His name is the LORD," and it is written after it, "a father of orphans and a judge of widows" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:10: And in the Yalkut (Isaiah, remez 488) further verses are brought: (Psalms 146:6-7), "who made heaven and earth," and so on, "who executes judgment for the oppressed," and it is written (Isaiah 66:1), "the heavens are My throne," and so on, "and to this one I look, to the poor and contrite of spirit"; "the LORD is King forever and ever" (Psalms 10:16) - what is written after it? "the desire of the humble You have heard, LORD," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:11: Further, they said in Sotah (5a), on the verse "and with the contrite and humble of spirit": Rav Huna and Rav Chisda - one said, "I am with the contrite" [as one word: "iti dakka"]; the other said, "I am, with the contrite" [i.e. "I dwell with"]. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "iti dakka" - I raise him up until he dwells with Me, and this is [alluding to] "I shall dwell with the contrite." "Ani et dakka" - I make My Shechinah recline beside him. And the reasoning follows the one who said "ani et dakka" [I am, with the contrite], for the Holy One, blessed be He, set aside all mountains and hills and rested His Shechinah on Mount Sinai, and Mount Sinai did not become exalted above [it did not grow]. Rav Yosef said, a person should always learn from the mind of his Creator, for the Holy One, blessed be He, set aside all mountains and hills and rested His Shechinah upon Mount Sinai, and set aside all fine trees and rested His Shechinah in the thornbush - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:12: Now, from the plain sense apparent in these teachings from Tractates Megillah and Sotah, one finds humility above in the first three [Sefirot] and in the Holy One, blessed be He, and further in the Shechinah, as shall be explained - for the place of pride is in the first three, as explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas, page 230a), that when David reached the three supernal Sefirot he opened and said (Psalms 131:1), "LORD, my heart is not proud, nor are my eyes haughty, and I have not walked in matters too great or too wondrous for me" - and this is what is said (Isaiah 57:15), "for thus says the High and Exalted One," and so on - and this matter is in Chochmah and Binah, as explained in the Zohar: "high" from Abraham [Chesed], "and exalted" from Isaac [Gevurah]. And likewise, "exalted and holy I dwell" is above, in the head of Arich [Anpin], where there is "holy," as explained in the Idra of Naso (page 134a). And likewise, "extol Him who rides upon the clouds, His name is the LORD," as this verse is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, page 165a), and it explains there that "He who rides upon the clouds" is the supernal Mother - see there. And further, in Tractate Sotah, that a person should learn from the mind of his Creator, that He did not rest His Shechinah [on the great], and so on - behold, humility is found in the Holy One, blessed be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:13: And the whole existence of humility is found more in the lower attribute, which is the Shechinah of the Holy One, blessed be He, and is called "moon" - and the moon is destined to be renewed, whose light diminished. And they said in Tractate Chullin (60b) that the Holy One, blessed be He, said to her, righteous ones shall be called by your name: Jacob the Small, Samuel the Small, David the Small - David, because he was a chariot for this attribute, would make himself small and say, "I am young and despised" (Psalms 119:141), because so, sometimes the moon is diminished; and sometimes he would exalt himself, "the utterance of the man raised on high," and so on (II Samuel 23:1). And so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Pekudei, page 232b), and it says there: and King David lowered himself before the Holy One, blessed be He, for whoever lowers himself before the Holy One, blessed be He, is raised above everyone - and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, was pleased with him in this world and in the World to Come. In this world: "and I will defend this city, for My sake and for the sake of My servant David" (II Kings 19:34); in the World to Come, as it is written (Hosea 3:5), "and they shall seek the LORD their God, and David their king," and so on - David is king in this world, and David shall be king for the time to come - and therefore it says (Psalms 118:22), "the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:14: Come and see, at the time the moon is stripped of her light and does not shine, then she is in poverty on all sides, and darkened, and has no light at all; and when the sun turns toward her and illuminates her, then she is adorned for him like a female adorned for a male, and then she rules in dominion over the world. And therefore David used to adorn himself in exactly this manner: sometimes he was poor, and sometimes he was in wealth, in the wealth of everything - and therefore he would say (Psalms 119:141), "I am young and despised," and yet, "I have not forgotten Your precepts." In this manner a person should lower himself in everything, to be a vessel that the Holy One, blessed be He, is pleased with - and this has already been established, as it is written (Isaiah 57:15), "and with the contrite and humble of spirit" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:15: And therefore the poor, whose heart is broken and crushed, are a chariot for this attribute - and so they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayikra, beginning of page 9) - these are its words: but come and see, no people of the world are found as close to the supernal King as these vessels He makes use of - and who are they? "A broken and crushed heart" (Psalms 51:19) and "the contrite and humble of spirit" (Isaiah 57:15) - these are the vessels of the King - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:16: And so it says in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, chapter 7), on the verse (Psalms 51:19), "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" - these are its words: Rabbi Abba bar Mariyon said, whatever the Holy One, blessed be He, disqualified in an animal, He made fit in a person: He disqualified in an animal one that is blind, or broken, or maimed, or has a wart, and He made fit in a person "a broken and crushed heart." Rabbi Alexandri said, this ordinary person, if he uses broken vessels, it is a disgrace to him - but the Holy One, blessed be He's vessels of use are broken ones, as it is said (Psalms 34:19), "the LORD is near to the brokenhearted," "the healer of the brokenhearted" (ibid. 147:3), "and with the contrite and humble of spirit" (Isaiah 57:15), "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, a broken heart" (Psalms 51:19) - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:17: And the general principle is that in all of Atzilut, humility is found at every level according to its aspect. In the Tikkunim (page 5b) they explained that the Shechinah is called "humility" - these are its words: and humility is bound with fear, this is what is written (Proverbs 22:4), "the reward of humility is the fear of the LORD" - whoever has fear of the LORD is brought by it to humility, which is the supernal Shechinah, whose "fear of the LORD" is a heel to her - and this is Moses's level, of whom it is said (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" - and because fear is a heel to her, the masters of the Mishnah established that fear is a small matter compared to Moses - to this point. And in the Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas, page 230a) they explained that Malchut is called "humility" - these are its words: and therefore the masters of the Mishnah established, study is not the essential thing, but rather the deed - because the Holy One, blessed be He, is hidden in the secrets of Torah; through what is He made known? Through the commandment, which is the Shechinah, which is His image - just as He is humble, His Shechinah is humility; He is pious, and she is pious, and so on - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:18: And further, humility is found even in the Keter, for the attributes of humility are for a person to overlook wrongs against himself and to be merciful, and the like, which are the Thirteen Attributes we recite, "God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abundant in kindness," and so on (Exodus 34:6), and likewise, "who is a God like You, who bears iniquity and passes over transgression for the remnant of His heritage" (Micah 7:18), which Rashbi explained in the Idra of Naso (page 131b) to be the thirteen attributes of mercy in Arich [Anpin]. Behold, everywhere you find His greatness, even above, in the place of pride, there you find humility - and therefore a person must resemble his Creator, overlooking wrongs against himself and [practicing] the other attributes mentioned concerning the Holy One, blessed be He, in His thirteen attributes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:19: And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in the Midrash (Yalkut, Parashat Eikev, siman 873, page 283, column 3) - these are their words: "to walk in all His ways" - these are the ways of the Omnipresent: "the LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abundant in kindness and truth" (Exodus 34:6), and it says (Joel 3:5), "whoever calls upon the Name of the LORD shall be saved" - and how is it possible for a person to be called by the Name of the LORD? Rather, the Omnipresent is called merciful and gracious, as it is said (Psalms 103:8), "merciful and gracious is the LORD" - you too be gracious, and give free gifts. The Omnipresent is called merciful, as it is said (Deuteronomy 4:31), "for the LORD your God is a merciful God" - you too be merciful. The Omnipresent is called righteous, as it is said (Psalms 11:7), "for the LORD is righteous, He loves righteousness" - you too be righteous. The Omnipresent is called pious, as it is said (Jeremiah 3:12), "for I am pious, says the LORD" - you too be pious. Therefore it is said, "and it shall be, whoever calls upon the Name of the LORD shall be saved," and it says (Proverbs 16:4), "the LORD has made everything for His own purpose" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:20: And I heard in the name of the Geonim that they said, with this intent, in Tractate Rosh Hashanah (17b), on (Exodus 34:6), "and the LORD passed before him and proclaimed" - Rabbi Yochanan said, were it not written in Scripture it would be impossible to say this: it teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, wrapped Himself like a prayer leader and showed Moses [the order of prayer], and said to him, whenever Israel do before Me according to this order, I shall forgive them - to this point. And this matter is difficult, for we see that many times we recite the Thirteen Attributes and are not answered. Rather, the Geonim say that the intent of "do before Me according to this order" is not only about wrapping in a tallit, but that they perform the order of the attributes that the Holy One, blessed be He, taught Moses, which is "God, merciful and gracious" - meaning, just as He is merciful, you too shall be merciful, and so on, for each of the Thirteen Attributes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:21: And my teacher, peace be upon him, wrote that besides the aspect of the Thirteen Attributes of mercy, which is the aspect of the thirteen repairs of the beard, explained to indicate humility, all the other repairs of Arich Anpin as well, designated by the terms head, forehead, eye, nose, mouth, and so on, all indicate His great humility toward the created beings.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:22: From the attribute of the Head is humility, for so it is said, "lowly of knee, and light to the head" - meaning that a person lowers his head before one greater than him; so too the attribute of Keter lowers itself before the Cause of All, and is called "Ayin" [Nothing], since it considers itself as nothing before the Emanator, and it lowers its head to watch over and bestow to those below, since all of them turn to nurse from it. And so it is fitting that a person consider himself as nothing before His greatness, blessed be He, which has no end or limit, as we elaborated in the Gate of Fear, chapters 1-2 - and of this Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said (Exodus 16:7), "and what are we?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:23: And so one can say, for this reason, that Chochmah is called MaH [what], as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Yitro, page 79b), "MaH is His name" - and besides the known reason, that it is the secret of the Name that equals MaH, being ADaM [man] - it is possible that for the reason mentioned it is called MaH, since it considers itself as nothing before its Emanator, along the lines of "and all the inhabitants of the earth are considered as nothing" (Daniel 4:32).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:24: And just as Keter is not prevented, by any blemish from those below, from bestowing its flow, which never ceases - so too a person, even if others sin against him, should not for this reason refrain from doing good, as we were commanded (Leviticus 19:18), "you shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge" - and it is already known what they, of blessed memory, explained (Yoma 23a) concerning vengeance and grudge-bearing. It follows that according to the law of the Torah, a person is obligated to be humble, and to have no resentment in his heart against his fellow.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:25: Second, in the Brain: one must free his thought from all confusion and revulsion, and be bound to Torah, just as thought is bound above to nurse - and concerning this Rashbi, peace be upon him, and his colleagues were careful never to interrupt their thought even for a moment, as is known.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:26: Third, in the Forehead: one must not harden his forehead, as it is said (Jeremiah 3:3), "and you had the forehead of a harlot woman," and so on - but rather draw a stream of goodwill toward every person, just as the supernal Forehead is called "the forehead of goodwill," through which the judgments in the lower worlds are appeased (Parashat Naso, page 129a) - so no quarrel or dispute shall be aroused from him toward any person, small or great, but rather everyone, even Gentiles, shall be pleased with him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:27: In the Eyes: one's eye must be open to have compassion on the poor and watch over them, just as of the supernal Eye it is said (Psalms 33:18), "behold, the eye of the LORD is upon those who fear Him, upon those who wait for His kindness," and likewise, "behold, He who guards Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps" (ibid. 121:3) - that He watches, oversees, and has mercy forever, and even if those below sin, He does not remove His merciful watch from them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:28: And so one must be generous and yielding with his money, and give with a good eye, and be "good of eye" - for above, of the supernal Eye it is said (Proverbs 22:9), "he who is good of eye shall be blessed" - and whoever merits this attribute shall live long, as they said in Tractate Megillah, chapter "Bnei Ha'ir" (28a): they asked Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah, through what have you lived long? He said, I was yielding with my money. And the reason is that whoever is exacting indicates the constriction that is judgment, in the secret of the "shattering" [of the vessels], but whoever is yielding indicates Chesed, which gives and yields even to one unworthy - and all the attributes of Arich indicate complete kindness and yielding without any exactingness at all, and there is the place of length of days - and therefore he lives long, measure for measure.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:29: And similarly to this they said of Job, that he was yielding with his money - they said in Bava Batra, first chapter (15b): Rabbi Yochanan said, greater is what is said of Job than what is said of Abraham - for of Abraham it is written (Genesis 22:12), "for now I know that you fear God," while of Job it is written (Job 1:8), "a man perfect and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil" - what is "and turns away from evil"? They said, Job was yielding with his money: the world's custom is [to charge] half a perutah [profit] to the shopkeeper - Job would yield this from his own [profit] - to this point. And one must say that "turns away from evil" means that he was good of eye, for whoever is stingy of eye is called "evil of eye," and since it says "turns away from evil," it means from stinginess and evil of eye, and he was "good," which is the opposite of evil - he was yielding with his money. And so Rabbi Frida, explained in Tractate Eruvin (54b), lived long - he lived four hundred years - because he did not become angry and taught the halachah to his student four hundred times.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:30: And so one must have lowered eyes, like the attribute of the supernal Eye, which is lowered and humble to bestow to the world - and we have further elaborated on the repair of the eyes in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 8.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:31: In the Ears: his ears shall be open to hear the voice of Torah, the voice of prayer, and the voice of the poor, to have mercy on them - but he shall not hear through them the voice of slander, idle talk, and other blemishing words, as explained in the Gate of Holiness. And if he hears his own disgrace, he shall not respond - for the Holy One, blessed be He, hides His ear from people's sins and does not repay them according to their measure - and of this they said in Sefer Heichalot (chapter 18, letter 4), the angels call the Holy One, blessed be He, "the insulted King" - and His insult is that He bestows goodness and life to the created beings, and with what He gives them, they sin before Him, and He endures and is insulted.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:32: In the Nose: he shall resemble the attribute of the supernal Nose, of which it is said (Isaiah 48:9), "I will restrain My anger for My praise's sake, that I not cut you off" - being slow to anger, and from it flow forth life and abundance to all the created beings - so shall he resemble His attribute, blessed be He, and no fury of anger shall go forth from him toward any person.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:33: In the Face: he shall resemble the attributes called "faces," of which it is said (Numbers 6:25), "may the LORD make His face shine upon you" - and he shall receive every person with a pleasant countenance, and not harden his face, God forbid, against any person, as his punishment shall be explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:34: In the Mouth: he shall resemble the attribute of the supernal Mouth, and not let curses, excommunications, bans, and words of insolence and harshness, or disparaging speech, come out of his mouth - for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi used to boast that he never excommunicated anyone in his days - these are its words in the Yerushalmi (Mo'ed Katan, chapter "Elu Meglachin," halachah 1): Rabbi Yehoshua sent for a certain man three times, and he did not come. He sent to him, were it not that I have never excommunicated a person in my days, I would excommunicate that man - for there are twenty-four matters for which one is placed under a ban for the honor of the Rabbi, and this is one of them: "and whoever does not come," and so on, "by the counsel of the princes and the elders, all his property shall be forfeited and he shall be separated from the assembly of the exile" (Ezra 10:8) - to this point. And from this a person shall learn not to let curses and abuse come from his mouth, but rather his tongue shall be gentle to all, small and great alike - and one who increases silence in worldly matters lives long, because he thereby resembles his mouth to the attribute of the supernal Mouth, and we have already elaborated on this in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 10; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:35: And although we have explained that a person must conduct himself according to the attribute of his Creator regarding humility, sometimes he must also conduct himself according to the attribute of judgment, against the wicked, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 139:21-22), "do I not hate those who hate You, LORD, and loathe those who rise against You? I hate them with complete hatred." And it is forbidden to have mercy on the wicked, as it is said (Proverbs 12:10), "and the mercies of the wicked are cruel." And so we find a deed that Rabbi Chanina did, that he did not have mercy on a wicked man - they said in Vayikra Rabbah (chapter 5, siman 6): Rabbi Ibo said, there was a story of a certain butcher in Tzippori who fed Israel carcasses and torn animals - once, on the eve of Yom Kippur, he ate and drank and became drunk, and went up to the roof and fell and died. The dogs began licking his blood, and they asked Rabbi Chanina whether it was permitted to drive them away from him. He said to them, it is written (Exodus 22:30), "and men of holiness," and so on, "and flesh torn in the field you shall not eat; you shall cast it to the dogs" - this man who robbed the dogs and fed Israel carcasses and torn animals, leave him, let them eat from their own [what was rightfully theirs] - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:36: And so sometimes one must rebuke whoever needs rebuke, as King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 17:10), "a rebuke enters deeper into a man of understanding," and so on. And likewise to discipline his son and his student, as it says (ibid. 13:24), "he who withholds his rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently." But he must be composed in mind, not angry, but rather think in his mind that the striking with which he strikes his son or his student is an act of kindness he performs for him, in order to draw him near to holiness and subdue the husk from him - and so they said (Arachin 16b), how many times was Akiva ben Yosef struck by me, and it only added love in me - to fulfill what is said (Proverbs 9:8), "rebuke a wise man and he will love you." And so King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 141:5), "let the righteous strike me in kindness, and rebuke me," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:37: And so, if he is angry at his fellow who wronged him, he should remember some good that his fellow did for him, so that his anger relax from him, and learn from the attribute of his Maker, as it is written in Tractate Berachot (54b): Rabbi Yochanan said, even at the time of the Holy One, blessed be He's anger, He remembers the righteous, as it is said (Genesis 19:29), "and it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham" - what remembrance? He remembered for Lot the silence Abraham kept when he said of Sarah, "she is my sister" (see Genesis 12:13), and he [Lot] knew and remained silent - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:38: And this is one of the Thirteen Attributes of mercy that the prophet mentioned in "who is a God like You" (Micah 7:18) - that one of them is "He shall subdue our iniquities" - the intent being that although it would have been proper for the litigants to go out to exact payment from whoever committed that sin, the Holy One, blessed be He, subdues them under His hand and remembers for him some good he did - so shall a person conduct himself with his fellow, remembering his good and subduing the sin he did to him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:39: Further, among the attributes of humility are the three things we have learned in Tractate Avot (chapter 5, mishnah 19): whoever has these three things is among the disciples of Abraham our father - a good eye, a lowly spirit, and a humble soul, and so on. And most commentators agree that "a good eye" is being content with what one has - and even if his fellow has more money than he, he is not envious of them, but rather his own little seems much to him, and others' [wealth], though little, seems much to him too, and he wishes them to have even more than he would wish for himself. And its opposite is "an evil eye" - his eye is stingy about what his fellow has, and his own, though much, seems little to him, while his fellow's, even if little, seems much to him - and this is envy, being envious of what his fellow has, and being of evil eye about what he himself has, and wishing to have little, provided his fellow have even less.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:40: "A lowly spirit" is great humility, and its opposite is pride, which is "a haughty spirit" - and we find pride called "spirit," as it says (Ezekiel 20:32), "and what comes into your spirit."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:41: "A humble soul" is distancing oneself from desire, not pursuing the fulfillment of one's desire in matters of foods and forbidden relations - and we find that desire is called "soul" [nefesh], as it says (Deuteronomy 12:20), "according to all the desire of your soul," and "whatever your soul asks of you" (ibid. 14:26). And "a wide [greedy] soul" is its opposite - one who pursues his desire, as it says (Ecclesiastes 6:7), "yet the soul [appetite] is not filled." And whoever pursues desire in foods and other matters, his heart becomes proud, as it is written (Deuteronomy 8:12-14), "lest you eat and be satisfied, and build fine houses and dwell in them... and your heart become proud, and you forget the LORD your God."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:42: This is the way Rambam explained it, and after him the rest of the commentators followed. And Rabbi Yitzchak Abravanel, in his commentary on the Mishnah, explained this matter and elaborated on it, saying that these three correspond to the three things mentioned by Rabbi Elazar HaKappar: envy, desire, and honor. Envy corresponds to "an evil eye," for his eye is evil regarding what belongs to others and he envies them - and this falls in the matter of money, until through this he comes to covetousness, robbery, theft, deceit, and all the transgressions bound up with the acquisition of money. Corresponding to desire is "a wide soul," which is excessive desire in intercourse, in foods, and in other forbidden matters. Corresponding to honor is "a haughty spirit," for when a person is proud and arrogant, he comes to disgrace his fellow and curse him, and to honor himself through his fellow's shame.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:43: And from the commentary of Rambam, and likewise the commentary of Rabbi Yitzchak Abravanel, it appears that their version of the Mishnah was "a good eye, a humble soul, and a haughty spirit," and these correspond exactly, in order, to envy, desire, and honor, as explained. But our version is not so, and likewise the version of the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him - rather, "a good eye, a lowly spirit, and a humble soul" - and this version appears to be primary, for the reason we shall explain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:44: And these three are found in Abraham our father, and their opposite in the wicked Balaam, and Rambam and Rabbi Yitzchak Abravanel explained them thoroughly; see there. And since it is not relevant to practical matters, we have not copied their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:45: And along our own way, these three attributes mentioned are found in His attributes, blessed and exalted be He, above, in His holy and pure Atzilut. "A good eye" is giving with generosity and abundance, and we have already explained above this aspect, that there is an attribute called "he who is good of eye shall be blessed," and this designation may be attributed to the first three [Sefirot], since their bestowal is with mercy and generosity - for it is known that Imma is called "the storehouse of free gifts," as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Devarim Rabbah 2:1) concerning "Va'etchanan" (Deuteronomy 6:23), that he asked from the storehouse of free gifts, of which it is said (Exodus 33:19), "and I shall favor whom I shall favor" - even though he is not fit or worthy.
